title: Graphiti (Zep)
by: Zep Software; open source. Read from the Graphiti README, its edge schema (graphiti_core/edges.py) and its edge resolution and invalidation code (graphiti_core/utils/maintenance/edge_operations.py), and the getzep/zep README. Then from help.getzep.com (v4): the llms.txt index, Facts, How Graph Creation Works, Source traceability and Manually Updating the Graph; and two Zep blog posts: 'How Zep Context Graphs keep two timelines for every fact' (2026-10-29) and 'How Zep tracks provenance in agent memory' (2026-07-14). The paper 'Zep: A Temporal Knowledge Graph Architecture for Agent Memory' (arXiv 2501.13956) was not read; only search summaries of its abstract were seen.
summary: A framework for a temporal knowledge graph of entities and facts, built from episodes (the raw data, kept verbatim). Every fact edge has valid_at and invalid_at (when it was true in the world) and created_at and expired_at (when the system learned it and when it learned it had ended), and lists every episode that produced, reaffirmed or invalidated it. A model decides whether a new fact contradicts an old one; then a date rule closes the older fact instead of deleting it. Zep, the hosted product, runs Graphiti in production.
ideas: Episodes are the ground truth, kept byte for byte. A fact's episode list grows with every episode that extracted, reaffirmed or invalidated it; when two entities merge, the node keeps both sides' episodes. Zep warns that this records where a fact came from, not that it is true.

Two timelines, four timestamps: valid_at and invalid_at (event time) and created_at and expired_at (system time). Asking 'what was true on date T' and 'what did the graph hold on date T' are separate queries.

Contradiction in two steps: a model compares the new fact with related facts; if it finds a contradiction, a date rule decides. When the new fact starts later, the old one gets invalid_at equal to the new valid_at and expired_at equal to now, and stays in the graph.

Order of arrival does not change the event timeline: if a backfill brings an older fact after the one that replaced it, the incoming fact is ended at the later fact's start. Only created_at and expired_at show the reading order. A fact arriving with an end date is stored already ended.

Dates come from each episode's reference_time, which resolves 'last week' in the text. A plan or deadline does not end a fact. Without reference_time the ingestion time is used, and on loaded history that can close the newer fact instead of the older.
Removing an episode deletes a fact or node only when no remaining episode supports it. Metadata set on an episode is projected onto everything derived from it, for search filters and access control.

Entity resolution prefers to under-merge: two nodes for one person are recoverable, a wrong merge is not. Entity and edge types can be declared up front (Pydantic models in Graphiti, a custom ontology in Zep). Manually added edges are compared with the graph only when deduplicate is true.
Per the paper's abstract as summarised in search results: Zep scores 94.8% on Deep Memory Retrieval (DMR) against MemGPT's 93.4%, and reports gains on LongMemEval.

took.idea: Every derived doc names all the raw records it came from, and the list only grows
Keep 'when it held' apart from 'when we wrote it'
A fixed date rule decides which of two conflicting docs holds once a conflict is named; a model may only propose the conflict
What holds depends on when things held, not on the order docs were written, so a late backfill gives the same answer
A derived doc goes away only when none of its sources remain
